meta.note: Exam-style written questions. Chapter 12 has 2 MCQs + Q3 T/F (Stage 2 intext) and 6 long-form exercises here.

questions.question: List two methods of producing magnetic fields.
hints: Think Oersted's discovery — current produces magnetism.
Permanent magnets also produce magnetic fields without current.
questions.model_answer:
Two methods of producing magnetic fields:

1. **Using a permanent magnet** (e.g. bar magnet).
2. **Passing electric current** through a conductor — such as a straight wire, circular coil, or **solenoid** (electromagnet).
marking_points: Current through conductor / solenoid / electromagnet mentioned
common_mistakes: Saying 'moving charge' without linking to current in conductor

questions.question: When is the force experienced by a current–carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field largest?
hints: Force depends on angle between current direction and magnetic field.
F = BIL sin θ — when is sin θ maximum?
questions.model_answer:
The force is **largest when the conductor is perpendicular to the magnetic field** (current direction ⊥ B).

Then θ = 90° and sin θ = 1, giving maximum F = BIL.

When the conductor is parallel to the field (θ = 0°), force is zero.
marking_points: When conductor/current is perpendicular to magnetic field
Reference to maximum sin θ or F = BIL

questions.question: Imagine that you are sitting in a chamber with your back to one wall. An electron beam, moving horizontally from back wall towards the front wall, is deflected by a strong magnetic field to your right side. What is the direction of magnetic field?
hints: Electron motion is opposite to conventional current direction.
Use Fleming's left-hand rule: thumb = force (deflection), forefinger = B, middle finger = current.
questions.model_answer:
Electron beam moves from **back → front** (towards you). **Conventional current** is opposite → from front to back.

Deflection is to **your right** (force on positive charge).

By **Fleming's left-hand rule**, magnetic field is **vertically downward** (into the floor / ground).
marking_points: Notes electron current is opposite to electron motion
common_mistakes: Using right-hand thumb rule instead of left-hand for force
Wrong vertical direction (up instead of down)

questions.question: State the rule to determine the direction of a (i) magnetic field produced around a straight conductor-carrying current, (ii) force experienced by a current-carrying straight conductor placed in a magnetic field which is perpendicular to it, and (iii) current induced in a coil due to its rotation in a magnetic field.
hints: (i) Right-hand thumb rule — thumb = current, curled fingers = B.
(ii) Fleming's left-hand rule — forefinger B, middle finger I, thumb F.
questions.model_answer:
(i) **Magnetic field around straight conductor:** **Right-hand thumb rule** — if the thumb points in the direction of current, the curled fingers show the direction of magnetic field lines around the wire.

(ii) **Force on conductor in ⊥ magnetic field:** **Fleming's left-hand rule** — stretch forefinger (field B), middle finger (current I), thumb gives force F on the conductor.

(iii) **Induced current in rotating coil:** **Fleming's right-hand rule** — forefinger = field, thumb = motion of conductor, middle finger = induced current.
marking_points: (iii) Fleming's right-hand rule for induced current
common_mistakes: Swapping left and right Fleming rules
Using thumb rule for force on conductor

questions.question: When does an electric short circuit occur?
hints: Short circuit = very low resistance path.
questions.model_answer:
A **short circuit** occurs when the **live wire and neutral wire come into direct contact** with each other **without passing through an appliance/load** (often due to damaged insulation or faulty wiring).

Resistance of the circuit becomes very small, so current **increases heavily**, overheating wires and tripping fuses/MCBs.
marking_points: Live and neutral in direct contact / bypassing load
Mention of insulation fault or faulty connection (optional)

questions.question: What is the function of an earth wire? Why is it necessary to earth metallic appliances?
hints: Earth wire is green; connected to metal body and ground.
If live wire touches casing, current goes to earth instead of through user.
questions.model_answer:
**Function of earth wire:** The **green earth wire** connects the **metallic body** of an appliance to the **ground** (deep inside Earth).

**Why necessary:** If the **live wire** accidentally touches the metal casing due to insulation failure, the large current flows to **earth** through the low-resistance earth path. The **fuse blows** and the user is protected from **severe electric shock**.
marking_points: Earth wire connects metallic body to ground
Prevents shock if live touches casing
Fuse blows / current diverted to earth
common_mistakes: Saying earth wire carries normal operating current
